title: Summit AI x Redwood — FP8/INT8 benchmark results readout + rollout plan
next_steps: Redwood to share the approved benchmark excerpt + methodology footnotes (H100/A100, prefill/decode mixes, variance controls).
Summit AI to confirm target model(s), context length range, and primary region(s) for a pilot (hosted vs dedicated).
Redwood to provide pilot benchmark runner instructions + container tags for reproducibility.
Schedule a 30-min follow-up to review pilot plan and agree on canary cohorts + rollback thresholds.
action_items: Avery Johnson: Send recap email with (1) numbers we can share externally, (2) rollout timeline, (3) security/compliance links requested.
Markus Klein: Share kernel-mode flag names + how to force baseline vs FP8 vs INT8 in the pilot environment.
Grace Kim: Package the 3-case Nsight trace bundle (attention-heavy, matmul-heavy, long-context) for Summit AI’s perf review (sanitized).
Jonas Weber: Share the quality sanity summary (what we measured, where FP8/INT8 is gated) and recommended eval prompts for Summit AI.
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-02-27
Time: 10:00am–10:53am PT
Duration: 53 minutes
Call type: Technical deep dive / results readout

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Avery Johnson, Markus Klein, Grace Kim, Jonas Weber
Summit AI: Priya Nair, Ethan Brooks, Marta Ionescu, Samir Qureshi

Auto-summary (Fireflies)
- Redwood walked through preliminary FP8 and INT8 performance results on H100 and A100 across mixed prefill/decode workloads.
- Discussed variance controls (clock pinning, driver/CUDA pinning) and what results are stable vs still being re-run.
- Reviewed quality caveats: a long-context regression risk on one model family under FP8, and INT8 sensitivity on summarization prompts.
- Outlined staged enablement: feature flags, per-model/per-region cohorts, perf canary, and automatic rollback triggers on TTFT/TPOT and error rates.

Topics
1) Benchmark methodology recap (workloads, metrics, stability)
2) H100 results (FP8 attention + INT8 matmul)
3) A100 results + “where it doesn’t help”
4) Quality + correctness guardrails
5) Rollout and rollback plan (flags + canary)
6) What we can share externally vs internal-only

Questions captured
- Can we force baseline kernels in a dedicated pool for A/B?
- Do you have per-token cost proxies or just tokens/sec?
- What are your rollback triggers and typical rollback time?
- For long-context prompts, do you automatically fall back to BF16/FP16?

Transcript

[00:00] Avery Johnson: Alright, we’re at the top of the hour. Thanks everyone. Today is basically the readout of the FP8/INT8 sprint numbers we’ve got so far, and then how we’d roll it out safely if you want to do a pilot. Markus and Grace are here for the runtime details, Jonas for evals.

[00:22] Priya Nair: Perfect. We’re mostly trying to decide if we push for H100 dedicated or if A100 is “good enough” with quantization. So, numbers and risk is what we need.

[00:34] Markus Klein: Yep. And quick note, we’ll keep it to the results we’re comfortable with, like runs that are stable. There are a couple cases we’re re-running because of driver mismatch noise earlier in the week.

[00:46] Ethan Brooks: That’s fine. We care more about the repeatable improvement and the guardrails.

[01:02] Avery Johnson: Great. Grace, do you want to start with the methodology recap, just so we’re aligned?

[01:10] Grace Kim: Sure. So we’re measuring end-to-end serving latencies, not just kernel microbench. Two main latency metrics: TTFT, time to first token, and TPOT, time per output token. We break it down by prefill and decode. We also track throughput in tokens per second, and then cost proxy as “GPU-seconds per 1M tokens” in our internal sheet.

[01:33] Grace Kim: The workloads are mixed: some prompts are short with medium generation, some are longer prompts, and we also do a tool-calling structured output variant. We run multiple seeds, warm-up iterations, and we pin GPU clocks on the runner for stability.

[01:51] Samir Qureshi: When you say pin GPU clocks, is that like application clocks or just max perf?

[01:56] Grace Kim: Application clocks, where allowed. In some clusters we can lock; in others we keep it consistent via the same MIG profile and container image. Earlier variance was partly because one region had a different driver/CUDA combo.

[02:15] Marta Ionescu: And are you measuring p95 on like aggregated traffic? Or per run?

[02:21] Grace Kim: Both. We report per run distribution, then aggregate across runs. For the readout here, I’ll call out p50 and p95 from the combined distribution. If it’s noisy, we’ll say “directional”.

[02:41] Avery Johnson: Awesome. Markus, can you walk through H100 first?

[02:46] Markus Klein: Yep. On H100, FP8 attention is where we see the most consistent decode wins, and INT8 matmul helps some models more than others depending on shape regimes.

[03:02] Markus Klein: For your likely workload—RAG-ish plus summarization—TTFT is dominated by prefill. FP8 attention doesn’t always improve TTFT because TTFT can be scheduler + launch overhead sensitive, not just pure kernel time.

[03:18] Ethan Brooks: That matches what we’ve seen. Sometimes the faster kernel makes it worse if it increases fragmentation.

[03:23] Markus Klein: Exactly. So we paired kernel changes with scheduler knob tuning: batching window and backpressure thresholds to keep prefill from starving decode.

[03:36] Grace Kim: For the top hosted model we tested in the “mixed” workload on H100, we saw TPOT improve roughly 10–18% p50, and 8–15% p95. TTFT was flat to slightly improved, like -2% to -6% in the stable cases.

[03:55] Priya Nair: And that’s with FP8 attention on?

[03:57] Grace Kim: That’s FP8 attention + INT8 matmul where eligible. But we don’t force INT8 for every shape; there are guardrails.

[04:08] Jonas Weber: Also, quality gating is per mode. We don’t just flip everything to FP8/INT8 globally.

[04:16] Ethan Brooks: Can you share absolute TTFT numbers or only relative?

[04:19] Avery Johnson: For external sharing we typically do relative deltas and footnotes. For a dedicated pilot under NDA, we can share more granular, but we still want to line it up with your prompt distribution so it’s apples-to-apples.

[04:33] Marta Ionescu: That’s fine. We mainly need to know if “15% faster” becomes “15% cheaper” in practice.

[04:39] Markus Klein: Usually it translates fairly directly into cost per token for decode-heavy workloads. For prefill-heavy, the scheduler and batching limit can matter more.

[04:52] Samir Qureshi: What about concurrency? Are these single-stream or loaded tests?

[04:56] Grace Kim: Both. We do single-request and then concurrency sweeps. The most representative is a concurrency level that matches our production traces—like 8 to 32 in-flight depending on model.

[05:11] Grace Kim: Under concurrency, the wins can shrink if you’re memory-bound or if batching changes. That’s why we report both.

[05:27] Priya Nair: Can you give me “H100 decode heavy” case? Like 2k prompt, 512 gen.

[05:33] Grace Kim: Yep. In that regime, the FP8 attention path is strong. In our runs, TPOT improved ~14% p50 and ~12% p95, with throughput up ~11–16%. TTFT is mostly neutral because you still pay the prefill.

[05:55] Ethan Brooks: And on A100?

[05:57] Markus Klein: A100 is a little more mixed. Some INT8 matmul paths help, but FP8 attention is not always supported the same way, and when it is, the win can be smaller.

[06:10] Grace Kim: A100 stable runs show TPOT improvements more like 6–12% depending on the model. Some cases are within noise if the workload is short-output, because the overhead dominates.

[06:25] Samir Qureshi: Noise meaning like run-to-run variance?

[06:27] Grace Kim: Yep. We set a variance threshold; if p95 moves around more than a few percent, we treat the difference as not significant. We’ll rerun those.

[06:41] Priya Nair: Okay. Now the elephant: quality. If we get 15% better and outputs get worse, it’s useless.

[06:48] Jonas Weber: Totally. Two buckets: correctness and quality. Correctness: we have shape guardrails and fallbacks. If a shape isn’t supported in INT8, we fall back automatically to baseline kernels.

[07:02] Jonas Weber: For quality: FP8 and INT8 can be fine, but there are known sensitive cases: long-context and certain summarization prompts, and also tool-calling JSON formatting can get a bit more brittle if the quantization profile is aggressive.

[07:19] Ethan Brooks: What do you mean by “brittle”? Like invalid JSON?

[07:22] Jonas Weber: Yeah. Slight increase in formatting errors on some models if you push INT8 in certain layers without calibration. That’s why we require calibration and we gate defaults behind an eval sign-off.

[07:37] Marta Ionescu: Is FP8 worse than INT8 for quality?

[07:40] Jonas Weber: It’s not strictly “worse”. FP8 can be very good for performance and generally stable, but we saw one model family where long-context responses had a measurable regression in our sanity suite. That one is currently gated: we won’t default FP8 above a context threshold, and we may keep it baseline for that family until we adjust.

[08:05] Priya Nair: Do you automatically fall back based on context length?

[08:09] Markus Klein: That’s in the heuristics. We can route by shape regime: hidden size, head dim, and seq-len. For long context beyond a threshold, we can keep BF16/FP16 or use a safer quant profile.

[08:26] Samir Qureshi: Is that a per-request decision? Or per deployment?

[08:30] Markus Klein: In our hosted runtime, it’s a per-request dispatch decision but controlled by server-side policy. For dedicated, we can do it either way: static config or dynamic dispatch with policy.

[08:46] Ethan Brooks: For the pilot, we’d want explicit A/B. Like half the traffic baseline, half FP8.

[08:51] Avery Johnson: Yep. We can do that. Markus, can you explain the flagging and canary stuff? That’s a big part of this call.

[08:59] Markus Klein: Sure. Everything is behind flags by model and by region (and by dedicated pool, if applicable). We start with a perf canary cohort: small percentage of requests or a small set of pods.

[09:14] Markus Klein: We monitor TTFT p95, TPOT p95, tokens/sec, GPU memory and utilization, plus error rate. If any metric breaches threshold relative to baseline for a sustained window, the system auto-rolls back to baseline kernels.

[09:31] Samir Qureshi: What are the thresholds? And how do you avoid false positives on small samples?

[09:35] Markus Klein: For this sprint we tuned thresholds per SKU because H100 noise differs from A100. Roughly, rollback triggers are like TTFT p95 +15% and TPOT p95 +10% relative to baseline, plus error rate +0.2% absolute. But we also require minimum sample size and we do a noise suppression window.

[09:58] Grace Kim: We had an example earlier in the week where a canary saw a TTFT spike in one region, and it rolled back within a few minutes. Root cause ended up being a scheduler interaction plus a problematic shape; we disabled FP8 for that shape and kept the rest.

[10:18] Priya Nair: That’s actually good to hear. So the rollback time is minutes?

[10:22] Rafael Mendes (Speaker label may be wrong): Typically under 5 minutes once it’s confident. (Sorry, I’m not on this call—ignore that.)

[10:27] Avery Johnson: Fireflies doing its thing. But yes, it’s minutes, not hours.

[10:34] Marta Ionescu: If it rolls back, do you notify customers?

[10:37] Avery Johnson: In hosted, it’s internal. In dedicated, we can coordinate with you depending on SLO impact. We also give you dashboards so you can see what mode you’re in.

[10:51] Ethan Brooks: Can we override to “baseline only” if we’re in an incident?

[10:55] Markus Klein: Yes. There’s an emergency override that forces baseline dispatch.

[11:03] Priya Nair: Okay. Let’s talk about cost. You mentioned GPU-seconds per 1M tokens. Do you have that for H100 with the FP8 path?

[11:12] Grace Kim: We do internally. The proxy shows ~8–14% reduction in GPU-sec per 1M tokens in decode-heavy workloads. But it’s not a billing metric; it’s a normalization.

[11:27] Avery Johnson: For dedicated, we can translate that into “how much headroom you get” in tokens/sec per GPU and what that means for instance count.

[11:36] Samir Qureshi: Any memory impact? Like KV cache bigger?

[11:39] Markus Klein: KV cache representation can change. We had an FP8 KV alignment edge case that caused perf weirdness; that’s fixed in the candidate release. In general, memory stays within a couple percent; the bigger impact is utilization and scheduling.

[12:00] Ethan Brooks: What about batch sizes? We typically run small batches, lots of concurrency.

[12:05] Grace Kim: That’s actually where scheduler tuning matters most. If batch sizes are tiny, kernel wins don’t realize fully. But in continuous batching, even “small batch” traffic can form batches.

[12:22] Priya Nair: I want to make sure we’re not just optimizing microbench. So, do you have end-to-end with tool-calling JSON output?

[12:29] Jonas Weber: Yes. We have prompt variants that enforce structured output. That’s where we saw a small increase in formatting errors under one INT8 profile. Our policy is: if structured output error rate increases beyond threshold, we gate INT8 or use a safer calibration.

[12:48] Marta Ionescu: Do you have a customer-facing statement on “quality risk”?

[12:52] Avery Johnson: We do, but it’s cautious. We’ll share the approved language: quantized modes are optional, validated on representative evals, and we provide fallback and canary protections. We don’t claim “no quality impact”.

[13:11] Priya Nair: That’s fair. Can we do our own eval set in the pilot?

[13:15] Jonas Weber: Please. We recommend you bring 200–500 prompts that match production. We can run them in A/B and compute deltas. We also have a small sanity suite to catch obvious regressions quickly.

[13:33] Samir Qureshi: Operationally, what’s the rollout sequence if we do dedicated?

[13:38] Markus Klein: Proposed: (1) baseline-only for a day to establish metrics, (2) enable FP8 attention on a small cohort, (3) add INT8 matmul where eligible, (4) expand cohort, (5) decide defaults. Each step has rollback.

[13:59] Ethan Brooks: And if we want to keep FP8 but not INT8?

[14:01] Markus Klein: Totally doable. They’re separate flags.

[14:06] Priya Nair: What’s the timeline? Like, when would this be generally available?

[14:12] Avery Johnson: Internally we’re targeting the runtime 1.22 release. For you, in a dedicated pilot we can do it earlier under controlled flags, assuming we align on the model and region.

[14:28] Marta Ionescu: Earlier meaning next week or like next month?

[14:31] Avery Johnson: Next week for a pilot setup is realistic if we keep scope tight. GA is a staged rollout over the following weeks.

[14:41] Priya Nair: Okay. One more: any vendor lock-in concerns? We’ve been evaluating vLLM directly.

[14:47] Markus Klein: Under the hood, we use our own runtime. But the knobs you care about—quant mode, batching, routing—are exposed in a predictable way. If you compare against vLLM/TGI, we can help you run the same prompts and distributions.

[15:05] Ethan Brooks: Cool. We also have Triton in-house for other workloads, but LLM serving is separate.

[15:11] Grace Kim: Yep. Triton’s great, but LLM attention + KV cache has its own set of gotchas.

[15:20] Priya Nair: Can you share the benchmark spreadsheet?

[15:23] Avery Johnson: We can share an excerpt and a snapshot. The full sheet includes internal model hashes and other details. We’ll export a customer-safe view with footnotes.

[15:36] Marta Ionescu: Footnotes like driver version and clocks?

[15:38] Grace Kim: Exactly: CUDA/driver, container tag, GPU clocks policy, and workload definition.

[15:49] Samir Qureshi: If we run in our VPC later, does the same runtime apply?

[15:53] Avery Johnson: That’s Redwood Private. Similar runtime, same flags, but the control plane is in your network. For now we’re focused on dedicated.

[16:05] Ethan Brooks: What do you need from us to kick off the pilot?

[16:08] Avery Johnson: Three things: target model(s), target region(s), and your success criteria—like “p95 TPOT improvement >= 10% without quality delta beyond X.”

[16:23] Jonas Weber: And an eval set, even if small at first.

[16:27] Priya Nair: Success criteria: we want at least 10% lower p95 TPOT, TTFT no worse than 5%, and no measurable increase in JSON failures. Quality: we can accept small changes but not worse summary factuality.

[16:46] Jonas Weber: Great. We’ll propose specific metrics: structured output validity rate, and a lightweight factuality check on a subset.

[16:57] Markus Klein: For rollback triggers, we can mirror your criteria or keep ours stricter.

[17:03] Samir Qureshi: Keep it strict initially.

[17:06] Avery Johnson: Sounds good. We’ll do strict thresholds and expand once stable.

[17:12] Marta Ionescu: Any known “do not use FP8” cases right now?

[17:16] Grace Kim: Yes: one shape regime on long context for that one model family. Also, any cluster with driver mismatch—we simply won’t enable. That’s part of our gating.

[17:30] Priya Nair: Okay. Can you send the list of constraints? Like head dim, alignment requirements.

[17:36] Markus Klein: Yep. I’ll send you the constraints and the fallback behavior. It’s basically “if not supported, it runs baseline automatically.”

[17:49] Ethan Brooks: Great. Then we’ll decide H100 vs A100 after the pilot numbers.

[17:55] Avery Johnson: Perfect. Let’s do recap and next steps.

[18:00] Avery Johnson: Redwood will send a recap with the approved results excerpt, methodology, and what we can claim. Markus will share flag names and how to force modes for A/B. Grace will package a couple traces and the “stable run” cases. Jonas will send quality sign-off criteria and recommended eval prompts.

[18:21] Avery Johnson: From your side, confirm models and regions, and send a small eval set (even 100 prompts to start). Then we’ll schedule a 30-minute follow-up to finalize the pilot plan and canary cohorts.

[18:34] Priya Nair: Works for us.

[18:36] Ethan Brooks: Yep, thanks.

[18:38] Samir Qureshi: Thanks all.

[18:41] Markus Klein: Thanks.

[18:42] Grace Kim: Thanks.

[18:43] Jonas Weber: Thank you.

[18:46] Avery Johnson: Alright, talk soon.
